reason: The word has a single figurative sense in the New Testament (something that trips a person up and brings them to ruin or sin), but the run renders it five ways: "stumbling block" in most chapters, and also "everything that causes stumbling", "cause for stumbling", "trap", "a rock that makes people fall" and "a rock to trip over". The last two translate the identical quoted phrase πέτρα σκανδάλου in Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8, which should match. An entry is needed to fix the default and state when the variants are allowed.
sense: figurative: something that trips a person up or ensnares them, causing a fall into sin, unbelief or ruin; also a person or thing that acts as such an obstacle

alternates.when: In the quoted phrase πέτρα σκανδάλου from Isaiah 8:14 (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8), where the paired λίθος προσκόμματος already takes the stumbling wording. Use the same rendering in both places.

Where σκάνδαλον stands beside πρόσκομμα and πρόσκομμα has already been rendered "stumbling block" (Romans 14:13). Not in Romans 11:9, where "snare" and "trap" are taken by παγίς and θήρα and σκάνδαλον keeps the default.
Where "stumbling block" is awkward in English: the collective πάντα τὰ σκάνδαλα in Matthew 13:41, which may include persons, and the abstract "there is no σκάνδαλον in him" in 1 John 2:10.

traditional: offence (KJV); stumbling block in most modern versions
rationale: In the Septuagint and the New Testament the word means a trap or an obstacle that makes someone fall, and figuratively whatever leads a person into sin or ruin. The older "offence" now suggests hurt feelings, and "hindrance" is too mild. "Stumbling block" is established English, conveys the image accurately, and is already what the run uses most often.
standard_view: Most modern translations (NIV, NRSV, ESV, NASB) use "stumbling block" in the majority of occurrences. They vary it with "cause of stumbling", "causes of sin", "temptations to sin", "hindrance", "obstacle" or "offense" in particular verses. In the Isaiah 8:14 quotation they have "rock of offense" (ESV, NASB) or "a rock that makes them fall" (NIV, NRSV). Lexicons give "trap", "temptation to sin or enticement", and "that which causes offense or revulsion"; the last is often applied to 1 Corinthians 1:23 and Galatians 5:11, where most versions nonetheless keep "stumbling block".
